hook.text: Babylonians tracked the sky on clay tablets over 3,000 years ago. They could predict eclipses centuries in advance.

buildup.text: They divided the sky into twelve constellations along the ecliptic—the origin of the zodiac signs we know today.

discovery.text: Their records span centuries. This long baseline of data let them spot patterns invisible in a single lifetime.

twist.text: They didn't explain why events happened—just when. Their astronomy was predictive math without underlying theory.

climax.text: Greek astronomers inherited Babylonian data. Without those centuries of records, Greek theories couldn't have emerged.

punchline.text: Three thousand years of records on clay. Prediction before understanding.

quiz.question: What did Babylonian astronomers contribute to modern astronomy?
options: Centuries of sky observations, the zodiac, and eclipse prediction methods
The first telescope designs and lens-grinding techniques
The theory that Earth orbits the Sun

details.summary: Babylonian astronomers (2000-500 BCE) were the first to systematically record celestial events on clay tablets, develop mathematical models for predicting eclipses and planetary positions, and divide the sky into constellations.
details.whyItMatters: Babylonian astronomy transformed sky-watching from casual observation into a mathematical science. Their systematic record-keeping and predictive models laid the foundation that Greek, Islamic, and eventually modern astronomy built upon.
takeaways: Babylonians systematically recorded celestial events on clay tablets
They developed mathematical models for predicting eclipses
Their base-60 system still gives us 360 degrees and 60-minute hours

faq.question: Could Babylonians really predict eclipses?
faq.answer: Yes. By tracking the Saros cycle — an 18-year, 11-day period after which nearly identical eclipses repeat — Babylonian astronomers could predict when eclipses would occur. Their clay tablet records span centuries, providing the data needed to discover this and other astronomical cycles.

faq.question: What is the MUL.APIN tablet?
faq.answer: A Babylonian astronomical compendium from about 1000 BCE listing stars, constellations, planetary periods, and intercalation rules. It's one of the most important astronomical texts from the ancient world, showing that Babylonians had organized, sophisticated astronomical knowledge centuries…
